Choreographic programming is well-known within the programming languages literature, which is the audience this README is intended for. The level of detail here is fine, not everything is written with being posted on news.ycombinator.com in mind.

To explain it briefly though, choreographic programming is a method of writing distributed programs that communicate in some message-passing fashion by -- rather than writing separate programs that communicate with send/recv and must be very intentionally designed to be in sync -- you have /one/ unified messaging primitive. In a typical distributed system, you might have something like A.send_to(B) / B.recv_from(A). In a choreographic system, you'd rather have something like A ~> B, where send_to and recv_from are /projected/ from ~> into separate programs during the process of compilation.

You might want this kind of abstraction for various reasons, but the biggest is that many choreographic systems offer a guarantee of deadlock-freedom. This isn't without tradeoff. At the moment, choreographic systems (and session types, another distributed abstraction) are very bad at handling any kind of failure / degraded performance over the network. There is active work within the PL community on resolving these issues, but for now, choreographic programming is primarily useful for prototypes, rather than production systems.

The difference is that in the past, technological development victimized only subsets of the work force. Mechanical looms were bad for textile workers, but good for everyone else. Personal computers were bad for "human calculators," but good for everyone else. The people who lost their jobs to technology could, theoretically, retrain and get another job.

But now we're facing technology that is theoretically capable of doing any job, at a price that's cheaper than any human. If you lose your job as a programmer due to AI, you can't just retrain as a lawyer, because those jobs are gone too (or will be soon). You can't just become a barista or a cab driver, those jobs are gone too.

Sniping at fellow working-class members is counterproductive. Ultimately, this is a test of democracy: can our government be forced to serve the people who it represents, or only corporate interests? If the latter, then we're entering a period of neo-feudelism.

text:
1. We prefer to be safe, and shut the burner off while going to take a leak.

We want to prevent scenarios like: you take a leak, the leak turns into a shitting session or a phone call, you forgot you left the burner on.

2. Most of the time my wife and I make food together so if one person needs to take a leak the other one is around.

3. We have a several thousand watt induction stove and boiling a pot of water takes a few minutes. You can take the leak, come back and turn on the burner and it'll be boiling in no time.

4. For long slow cooking, we have plenty of comfy seating in the kitchen/dining area where we can get work done while being in sight of pots.

5. We have 2 pets we'd need to locate in an emergency, and so we tend to put electrical and fire safety higher than most people.
